paras: The threatened lynching of Thomas Vaughn occurred in Swedesboro, New Jersey, on May 7, 1903, after Vaughn, a Black man from Philadelphia, was accused of shooting his wife on the town's main street. Townspeople threatened to lynch him on the spot, but the threats were discouraged and he was taken to jail at Woodbury.
Vaughn, described as 25 and from the South, had married his wife, Martha, at Swedesboro a year earlier, and the couple "had not lived happily together."

On Thursday morning the two met on the street and, according to the Monitor-Register, he shot her in the head during a quarrel, then stood by until about half a dozen men, including Justice of the Peace Stratton, seized him. The shooting "caused the greatest excitement," the Gloucester County Democrat's Swedesboro correspondent wrote, "and there were threats made to lynch him on the spot." Efforts by "hot-headed ones" to take the law into their own hands were quickly discouraged by persons the Monitor-Register did not name. Constable Harry Sparks, Justice Stratton and Frank Bachman took Vaughn to Woodbury on the same train that carried his wife to Cooper Hospital in Camden.

Vaughn was committed without bail on a charge of assault and battery with intent to kill. His wife, first reported dead, was recovering a week later with the bullet still in her head; no report of an indictment or trial was found.

The two local white weeklies that covered the episode treated it as a domestic shooting. The Monitor-Register's front-page headline on May 8 read "Jealous Husband Shoots His Wife," with the deck "Thomas Vaughn, a Swedesboro Negro, Tries to Murder His Better Half." Both it and the Democrat, on May 14, gave the lynching threats one sentence and stressed that Vaughn had been "safely" jailed. The Democrat's follow-up, "Not a Murder, Perhaps," described the wife's parents as "very respectable colored people" and remarked of her leaving home, "this is her reward."
The Monitor-Register described a .22-calibre revolver and named the wife Martha Bird, 18, while the Democrat reported a .32-calibre bullet and named her parents as James and Annie Burge.

bases: The only collective violence reported is townspeople's threats to lynch Vaughn on the spot after he was seized for shooting his wife; no attack on him followed (A1, A2).
Vaughn was threatened with lynching for the shooting but was not harmed and was taken safely to jail (A1, A2); the number of those threatening is not given.
Two separate local weeklies, the Monitor-Register of Woodstown and the Gloucester County Democrat of Woodbury, independently report the shooting and the threats to lynch (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Democrat Swedesboro correspondent
accounts.gist: The attempt caused the greatest excitement and threats to lynch him on the spot, but he was safely taken to jail on the same train as his wife.

accounts.label: Democrat follow-up
accounts.gist: Corrected an earlier report that the wife had died; she was recovering with a .32-calibre bullet in her brain.

framing.detail: Monitor-Register headline 'Jealous Husband Shoots His Wife / Thomas Vaughn, a Swedesboro Negro, Tries to Murder His Better Half'; threats attributed to 'hot-headed ones' whose efforts were discouraged.
